data.title: A site that looks like a page from a notebook
data.excerpt: Why a personal site works better as one sheet of paper than as a stack of cards, and the three rules that keep it that way.

children.text: Most personal sites are a grid of identical cards. They are tidy, and they all feel the same. This one is built around a different idea:
it is one page of a notebook
, and everything on it has to look like it belongs on that page.
That sounds vague, so I turned it into rules I could check against.
Three rules
Anything made by hand is pen and wash. Borders, rules and underlines are drawn, not drawn
at
with CSS.
Anything that is not hand-made is taped in as a print. Screenshots, photos, the avatar.
Type is the only other thing allowed: a text face, a typewriter face for labels and numbers, and a handwritten face for the odd margin note.
If a new element does not fit one of those, it does not go on the page. That one constraint killed more bad ideas than any design review.
The grain does a lot of work
A flat colour feels like a screen. A faint paper grain printed over the whole sheet, including the images taped to it, makes it feel like an object. It costs one pseudo-element and no extra requests.
A constraint you can check is worth ten you can only feel.
What I would do again
Start from the rules, not the layout. Once the rules held, the layout mostly fell out of them, and adding a new kind of content stopped being a design problem.

data.title: Notes on building a Worker that does one thing
data.excerpt: Small Cloudflare Workers age better than clever ones. A few habits that keep them boring in the good way.

children.text: The Workers I still trust a year later all have something in common: they do exactly one job and you can describe it in a sentence.
Keep the entry point thin
The
fetch
handler should read the request, call a function, and return a response. Everything interesting lives in plain functions you can test without a runtime.
Bindings are the interface
Treat
Env
as the contract. If a function needs a bucket and a database, it should say so in its arguments, not reach for a global. Tests then pass in small fakes and nothing else changes.
Decide what happens when it fails

Every network call can fail, and a Worker has no one watching it. For each one, pick out loud: retry, return a cached value, or fail fast with a clear status. The worst option is the one you did not choose.
Log one line per request
Method, path, status, duration. That is usually enough to find the problem, and it stays readable when traffic grows.

data.title: A short checklist before you ship a side project
data.excerpt: Ten minutes of boring checks that save you a week of embarrassment after launch.

children.text: Side projects usually ship late and then break in a way you would have caught in ten minutes. This is the list I run before pressing the button.
The page
Open it on a phone, on a slow connection, with the cache cleared.
Check the title, description and share image by pasting the link into a chat.
Tab through it with the keyboard once. If you get lost, so will other people.
The edges
What does it show when there is no data? An empty screen reads as broken.
What happens on a 404, and on an error you did not expect?
Is there a way to contact you that is not a form you will forget to check?
The part nobody does
Write the first paragraph of the README as if you were explaining the project to a friend. If that paragraph is hard to write, the landing page will be hard to read too.
Then ship it. A project that is live and slightly rough teaches you more than one that is perfect and private.

data.title: Local-first, in plain words
data.excerpt: Your data lives on your device, in files you can open without the app. Everything else follows from that.

children.text: "Local-first" sounds like a movement. It is really one decision:
the copy on your device is the real one.
The server, if there is one, is a convenience.
What that buys you
The app opens instantly, because it is not waiting on a network.
It works on a plane, in a tunnel, and when the company behind it disappears.
You can leave. Your notes are files, so another app can read them.
What it costs

Sync becomes your problem. When two devices edit the same thing, somebody has to decide what the result is. You can avoid the hard cases by keeping data in plain files and letting the operating system and a sync service move them, but you will meet the edge cases eventually.
A test I like
Delete the app and look at what is left. If you can still open and read your own work, the app was a tool. If you cannot, it was a landlord.
I do not think every app should be local-first. But for things people write, think and keep, it is the right default.

data.title: Docs are part of the feature, not the cleanup
data.excerpt: If you write the docs after the code, you document what you built. If you write them first, you notice what you should have built.

children.text: There is a trick that makes small features better: write the documentation paragraph
before
you write the code.
Why it works

Documentation forces you to explain the feature to someone who has not seen it. If the explanation needs three caveats, the feature has three design problems. It is much cheaper to find them in a paragraph than in a pull request.
The format
Keep it small. One paragraph that says what it does and why you would use it, then one example you could paste into a terminal.

content.code:
mytool sync --dry-run
# 3 files would change, nothing was written

children.text: If the example needs setup, the setup is part of the feature and belongs in the same page.
After you ship
Re-read the page as if you were new. Anything you skim past because "everyone knows that" is a gap. Fix it while the code is still fresh in your head.

data.title: Tabular figures and other small type decisions
data.excerpt: Four typographic details that cost almost nothing and quietly make a page feel finished.

children.text: You rarely notice good typography, and you always notice when it is missing. These are the cheap details I reach for first.
Tabular figures
Numbers in a list, a table or a date column should line up. Most modern fonts have tabular figures, and in CSS it is one line:
Without it,
is narrower than
and columns jitter as values change.
Optical sizing
A font designed for large sizes has tighter spacing and finer details than the same font at body size. If your font has an optical size axis, leave
font-optical-sizing
on
auto
and let it work.
Balanced headings
Long headings that leave one word on the last line look like a mistake.
One weight per job
Pick a weight for titles and a weight for body text and stop. Three weights on one screen reads as noise.
None of this is dramatic. That is the point.
